name: Sea buckthorn oil

lead: Sea buckthorn oil is taken from the berry pulp and seeds of a hardy shrub of Europe and Asia. The pulp oil is orange to deep red, rich in carotenoids and palmitoleic acid. It goes into creams, lotions and supplements promoted for moisturising, glow and skin repair.

Proponents credit carotenoids, vitamin E, sterols and unsaturated fatty acids for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Lab work on human skin cells found seed oil altered lipid changes induced by UV exposure. Published human trials cover dry eye and other mucosal conditions; a skin-aging trial was registered in 2008 but published skin results were not found.

paras: People use it as an ingredient in creams and serums, as a few drops of oil on skin, or as an oral supplement. Pulp oil can tint skin and fabric orange. Results are generally assessed over weeks.

Reviews describe the oil as generally well tolerated in the trials cited, but safety data specific to cosmetic use are limited. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and food supplement; regulatory status varies by country.

angle.text: Sea buckthorn oil supplies carotenoids and unsaturated fatty acids with antioxidant activity, and is used in creams and supplements for moisturising, glow and skin repair. Human trials have mostly covered dry eye and mucosal dryness.

lead: Sea buckthorn oil is a golden-orange to red oil obtained from the berries, seeds and sometimes leaves of the shrub Hippophae rhamnoides (now also classed as Elaeagnus rhamnoides), native to cold-temperate Europe and Asia.[1][2][3] It is used in creams, lotions, hair products and dietary supplements, where it is marketed for skin repair, hydration, a healthier-looking complexion and anti-aging.[2][3]

Pulp oil and seed oil differ in composition: pulp oil is rich in palmitoleic acid and carotenoids, whereas seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids.[4][5] Its carotenoids, tocopherols and sterols are the basis for its use in skincare, and a laboratory study found seed oil modified UV-induced changes in lipid metabolism in cultured human skin cells.[1][6]

Human trials of the oil have mostly examined oral use for dry eye and mucosal dryness; one trial of oral and topical use on skin aging was registered in 2008.[7][8][9] Reviews describe much of the other evidence as preclinical.[5]

paras: Sea buckthorn is a spiny, deciduous, suckering shrub of the family Elaeagnaceae that grows 2 to 5 m tall and bears bright orange berries 6 to 8 mm across.[3] It is native across cold-temperate Eurasia, from the North Sea and Baltic coasts to the Himalayas and northern China, and about 3.0 million hectares exist worldwide, mostly in China.[3] The genus name combines Greek words for horse and light, reflecting the ancient practice of feeding the leaves to horses to brighten their coats.[3] The berries contain about 400 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, plus vitamins E and K and several carotenoids.[3]

Reviews describe the oil as containing a wide range of active compounds including carotenoids, tocopherols, sterols, and polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids.[4][5] Reference sources report pulp oil at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent of the fruit and seed oil near 11 percent of seed weight, with beta-carotene the main carotenoid.[3] The fatty acid profile of developing berries and the mature seed has been characterised in detail,[10] and the oil has been compared with other unconventional plant oils for cosmetic use.[11] Its xanthophylls have been studied for bioaccessibility.[12] Wikipedia notes that the pomace left after pressing can be used to yield oil or a yellow-orange food colouring.[3]

Sea buckthorn oil is incorporated into hand creams, shampoos, massage oils and moisturisers.[3] Marketing and reference accounts credit it with moisturising, soothing and anti-aging effects; the Grokipedia entry additionally describes wound- and burn-healing claims, which that source attributes to reviews.[2] Laboratory work found that seed oil modified UV-induced changes in lipid metabolism in cultured human skin cells.[6]

Accounts describe use of the fruit and oil in Tibetan, Chinese, Mongolian and Russian traditional medicine for wounds, burns and digestive complaints.[2] The oil is also used as a food colourant and supplement.[2] Reviews have discussed possible health effects of its fatty acids and compounds, including cardiovascular and anticancer research, much of it preclinical.[5][13][14]

Sea buckthorn oil appears in hand creams, shampoos, massage oils and moisturisers.[3] Proponents point to palmitoleic acid and carotenoids as reasons it is used for dry or irritated skin. Reviews of its fatty acids discuss effects on human health in general terms.[4] A cosmetics-oriented comparison of unconventional plant oils examined its fatty acid profile for cosmetic use.[11] The seed oil study in keratinocytes and fibroblasts examined whether the oil protected skin cells from UV-induced changes, in cell culture only.[6]
Wikipedia and general reference accounts do not give safety information for the oil; it is used as a food colourant and supplement as well as a cosmetic ingredient.[2][3]

A double-blind randomised trial of 86 completers examined 2 g daily of oral sea buckthorn oil for three months against placebo in people with dry eye, assessing tear osmolarity and symptoms; its title reports that the oil attenuated tear film osmolarity and symptoms.[9] A companion trial examined oral sea buckthorn oil's effects on tear film fatty acids in dry eye.[15]

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include oral and topical treatment for skin aging (n=60, status unknown), effects on mucous membranes (n=116), dry eye (n=100), and eye health with lutein.[7][8][16][17] A flavonol-focused human study examined absorption and cardiovascular risk markers using sea buckthorn products, and a randomised crossover trial in overweight women examined sea buckthorn and bilberry effects on serum metabolites.[14][18] A 2024 in vitro study examined the oil's effect on muscle precursor cell proliferation.[19] No published results of the skin-aging trial and no controlled published trial on facial appearance were found.
